status: in progress — chapters 1-55 indexed (13-27 selectively); 56-66 pending
note: Indexed in sections along the book's standard seams: the oracles concerning Judah and Jerusalem (1-12), the oracles against the nations and the Isaiah apocalypse (13-27), the woes and the Hezekiah narratives (28-39), the Book of Comfort (40-55), and the closing chapters (56-66). The Scriptural Appendix cites Isaiah 5 for C11 and 56:1-7 for C27 and Shedding Harshness; the indexing order expected C03 and C27.
sectioning_note: As with Jeremiah, the status field names what is done.
coverage_note: Chapters 1-12, unindexed: the finery of the daughters of Zion (3:16-4:1), the branch and the canopy (4:2-6), the invading nation (5:26-30), the Assyrian razor (7:18-25), Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz (8:1-10), the remnant oracle (10:20-34), and the conquests of 11:14-16. Chapters 13-27 are indexed selectively, as Jeremiah 46-51 was: the oracles against Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Cush, Egypt, Dumah, Arabia, and Tyre (13, 14:1-2 and 14:22-32, 15, 16:12-14, 17, 18, 19:1-15, 20, 21:1-5 and 21:16-17, 23:1-14) anchor nothing in personal formation on a plain reading, and allegory was declined. Within them the index carries what does anchor: Moab's refugees and the prophet's tears for Moab, Egypt and Assyria named God's people, the bread brought to fugitives in Arabia, and Tyre's wages turned from storage to provision. Chapters 28-39, unindexed: the woe on Ariel's siege (29:1-8), the oracle on the animals of the Negev (30:6-7) and the theophany against Assyria (30:27-33), the woe on reliance on Egypt (31), which repeats 30:1-17, the first half of chapter 33, and the judgment on Edom (34). Chapters 40-55, unindexed: the trial of the nations and the raising of Cyrus (41:1-7 and 41:21-29), the battle-hymn of 42:10-17, the oracle of 44:24-28, and the oppressors' end in 49:22-26.

entries.pericope: The ox knows his owner… but Israel doesn't know, my people don't consider
entries.connection: The indictment opens with a comparison that shames: the ox knows its owner and the donkey its master's crib, 'but Israel doesn't know, my people don't consider.' Not ignorance of fact but a failure to attend, which is C07's diagnosis of the clouded eye. The body is sick from head to foot — 'wounds, welts, and open sores… not bandaged' — the condition C21's physician sets out to trace.

entries.pericope: Learn to do well. Seek justice. Relieve the oppressed… Though your sins be as scarlet
entries.connection: God refuses the worship of people whose 'hands are full of blood': sacrifices, festivals, and 'many prayers, I will not hear.' Religion without the doing, which is C04's hearer who is not a doer, measured exactly as James 1:27 measures it: 'Learn to do well. Seek justice. Relieve the oppressed. Judge the fatherless. Plead for the widow' — C16's list. And the offer that follows the indictment rather than replacing it: 'Come now, and let us reason together… Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.' C19's door.

entries.pericope: Your silver has become dross… I will thoroughly purge away your dross
entries.connection: 'How the faithful city has become a prostitute!' The princes love bribes and the widow's cause never reaches them — C16's corruption of authority. The judgment is described as refining: 'I will… thoroughly purge away your dross, and will take away all your tin. I will restore your judges as at the first.' C25's formation by fire, applied to a city.

entries.pericope: They shall beat their swords into plowshares
entries.connection: All nations streaming to the mountain to be taught — 'he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths' — and the instruments of war turned into tools for farming: 'nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.' C15's peace as something built, here built out of the very weapons, and C27's circle drawn around every nation. 'House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of Yahweh.'

entries.pericope: The loftiness of man shall be bowed down… Stop trusting in man
entries.connection: A land full of silver, gold, horses, chariots, and idols, and a day coming 'for all that is proud and haughty' — the cedars, the towers, the ships, 'all pleasant imagery.' Men will throw their idols of silver to the moles and bats. 'Stop trusting in man, whose breath is in his nostrils; for of what account is he?' C22's humility and C18's release from what one has built and accumulated.

entries.pericope: What do you mean that you crush my people, and grind the face of the poor?
entries.connection: God enters into judgment with the elders and leaders: 'It is you who have eaten up the vineyard. The spoil of the poor is in your houses. What do you mean that you crush my people, and grind the face of the poor?' C16's standard — that authority is measured by what it does for the vulnerable — applied to rulers who have done the reverse.

entries.pericope: He looked for justice, but, behold, oppression
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix names Isaiah 5 for C11: 'the vineyard planted for justice that yielded bitter fruit — the failure against which Christ calls Himself the true vine.' Everything was done for the vineyard — dug, cleared, planted with the choicest vine, a tower, a winepress — 'What could have been done more to my vineyard?' And it yielded wild grapes. The punchline is a pun in Hebrew: he looked for justice (mishpat) and found bloodshed (mispach), for righteousness (tsedaqah) and heard a cry (tse'aqah). C12's test of fruit, failed by the vine itself.

entries.pericope: Woe to those who join house to house, who lay field to field, until there is no room
entries.connection: 'Woe to those who join house to house, who lay field to field, until there is no room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land!' Accumulation that consumes the neighbour's place and ends in solitude: 'many houses will be desolate, even great and beautiful, unoccupied.' The Heavenly Palace asks a household in surplus to resist expansion and redirect toward the afflicted; this is the expansion, and its cost to those displaced and to the one who displaces them. Medium, as with Ecclesiastes 2:1-11, because the redirection is not described, only its absence.

entries.pericope: Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil… Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes
entries.connection: A series of woes: on those who drink from morning to night and 'don't respect the work of Yahweh'; on those who 'call evil good, and good evil; who put darkness for light' — C07's lens inverted; on those 'wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight,' the opposite of C02's teachability; on those who 'acquit the guilty for a bribe.' 'My people go into captivity for lack of knowledge.'

entries.pericope: Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips
entries.connection: The vision of the throne, the seraphim, 'Holy, holy, holy,' and the prophet's first words: 'Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King.' C04's mirror in its source form — self-knowledge produced by seeing holiness, not by comparing oneself with others. The coal touches the lips and the sin is taken away before the call is given (C19). The commission includes the hardest sentence in the prophets, which Jesus quotes: 'you see indeed, but don't perceive' — C07's blindness as a judgment that can be pronounced.

entries.pericope: Be careful, and keep calm. Don't be afraid… If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established
entries.connection: The king's heart and his people's 'trembled, as the trees of the forest tremble with the wind.' The prophet's message: 'Be careful, and keep calm. Don't be afraid, neither let your heart be faint.' And its condition, a play on the same Hebrew word: 'If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established.' C22's quiet soul offered to a frightened ruler, who refuses even the sign. The sign is given anyway: 'the virgin will conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel' — God with us, C19's ground.

entries.pericope: Don't say, A conspiracy! concerning all about which this people say, A conspiracy!
entries.connection: The prophet is warned 'not to walk in the way of this people': not to name conspiracies where they name them, not to fear what they fear — 'Yahweh of Armies is who you must respect as holy. He is the one you must fear.' 1 Peter 3:14-15 quotes it for Christians among hostile neighbours, which is C17's posture. And a test for voices: 'shouldn't a people consult with their God? Should they consult the dead on behalf of the living? Turn to the law and to the testimony!' — C08's. 'I will wait for Yahweh, who hides his face.'

entries.pericope: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light… Prince of Peace
entries.connection: 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.' The yoke broken, the boots of war burned, and a child born whose names include 'Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end.' C19's light dawning in the darkness, and C15's peace established 'with justice and with righteousness.'

entries.pericope: The bricks have fallen, but we will build with cut stone
entries.connection: After disaster, pride doubles down: 'The bricks have fallen, but we will build with cut stone. The sycamore fig trees have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place.' 'Yet the people have not turned to him who struck them.' C22's healing measured by what a person does after a fall; here the fall becomes the occasion for a grander building. The refrain — 'his hand is stretched out still' — ends at the decree-writers who 'rob the poor… that widows may be their spoil,' C16's corrupt authority.

entries.pericope: Should an axe brag against him who chops with it?
entries.connection: Assyria is God's rod and does not know it: 'By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom.' The answer is an image of absurdity: 'Should an axe brag against him who chops with it? Should a saw exalt itself above him who saws with it?' C22's humility as accurate self-knowledge — the instrument mistaking itself for the hand — and C16's warning to power that forgets it is held on loan.

entries.pericope: He will not judge by the sight of his eyes… with righteousness he will judge the poor
entries.connection: The shoot from Jesse's stump, with the Spirit of wisdom, counsel, knowledge, and fear of Yahweh resting on him. His justice is defined against appearances — 'He will not judge by the sight of his eyes, neither decide by the hearing of his ears; but with righteousness he will judge the poor' — which is C16's ruler. Then the peaceable kingdom: the wolf with the lamb, the child at the viper's den, 'They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain,' and old rivals reconciled — 'Ephraim won't envy Judah, and Judah won't persecute Ephraim.' C15's peace at the scale of creation. The conquests of 11:14-16 are not indexed.

entries.pericope: Though you were angry with me, your anger has turned away and you comfort me
entries.connection: The song of the redeemed: 'I will give thanks to you, Yahweh; for though you were angry with me, your anger has turned away and you comfort me… With joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation.' C19's turning and C10's joy, sung in the first person.

entries.pericope: You said in your heart, I will ascend into heaven… I will make myself like the Most High
entries.connection: A taunt-song over the fallen king of Babylon, 'who struck the peoples in wrath with a continual stroke… who didn't release his prisoners to their home.' His self-description is the anatomy of pride: 'You said in your heart, I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God… I will make myself like the Most High!' And the dead kings greet him in Sheol: 'Have you also become as weak as we are?' C22's humility as accurate self-knowledge, inverted, and C16's tyranny. The long tradition of reading 14:12 as the fall of Satan is not adopted; the text names its subject as the king of Babylon.

entries.pericope: Hide the outcasts! Don't betray the fugitive!… My heart sounds like a harp for Moab
entries.connection: Two movements of mercy toward an enemy nation. Moab's refugees are at the fords, and the command is given on their behalf: 'Hide the outcasts! Don't betray the fugitive! Let my outcasts dwell with you!' — and a throne promised that is 'established in loving kindness,' with one on it 'in truth,' mercy and truth together. Then the prophet weeps over Moab's ruin: 'I will water you with my tears, Heshbon… my heart sounds like a harp for Moab.' Shedding Harshness is measured by the movement in the chest at news of someone's downfall; the prophet's movement over an old enemy's downfall is grief. C16's refugee and C27's widened circle.

entries.pericope: Blessed be Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance
entries.connection: The two great oppressors of Israel's history are named with the titles of Israel itself: 'Blessed be Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.' A highway from Egypt to Assyria, the enemies worshipping together, and Israel 'the third with Egypt and with Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth.' C27's circle at its most startling, with no one left outside — the same movement as Psalm 87 and Isaiah 56, and tagged as they are, at medium, because the widening is God's and the practice is its human imitation.

entries.pericope: Watchman, what of the night?
entries.connection: 'I stand continually on the watchtower in the daytime, and every night I stay at my post.' A watchman set to see and report, and the question from the dark: 'Watchman, what of the night?… The morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire. Come back again.' C20's watchman, whose vigilance is a post held rather than a feeling kept up. PR12 shares the image but the watch here is for news, not for the movements of a heart, and it is not tagged.

entries.pericope: They brought water to him who was thirsty… met the fugitives with their bread
entries.connection: In a brief oracle on Arabia, a single act recorded: 'They brought water to him who was thirsty. The inhabitants of the land of Tema met the fugitives with their bread. For they fled away from the swords.' Strangers feeding strangers in flight. C16's care for those with no claim.

entries.pericope: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die
entries.connection: Jerusalem under siege prepares its walls and water supply 'but you didn't look to him who had done this' — C07's failure to see. The Lord calls to weeping and sackcloth, 'and behold, joy and gladness… Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die.' A call to return answered with a party, which is C19's door declined. The prophet's own response is grief that refuses easy comfort: 'Look away from me. I will weep bitterly. Don't labor to comfort me.'

entries.pericope: Who has you here, that you have dug out a tomb here?… cutting himself out a tomb on high
entries.connection: The royal treasurer Shebna is caught carving himself a grand tomb in the rock: 'What are you doing here?… Cutting himself out a tomb on high, chiseling a habitation for himself in the rock!' A monument to his own name, built while the city is under threat. The Hidden Life is the practice against the reach for an audience, and this is the reach carried into the grave. He is replaced by Eliakim, who 'will be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem' — C16's authority as service. Medium, as with Babel, because the passage is about one official's self-display and the practice is broader.

entries.pericope: Her merchandise and her wages will be holiness to Yahweh. It will not be treasured nor laid up
entries.connection: At the end of an oracle against Tyre, the great merchant city, a reversal of its whole economy: 'Her merchandise and her wages will be holiness to Yahweh. It will not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise will be for those who dwell before Yahweh, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing.' Profit not stored but redirected to others' food and clothing. The Heavenly Palace's positive form — surplus turned away from accumulation toward provision — in a prophecy rather than a command, and with its recipients named as 'those who dwell before Yahweh' rather than the poor; medium for both reasons. The first passage in the index to show the practice done rather than its absence costed.

entries.pericope: As with the servant, so with his master… as with the creditor, so with the debtor
entries.connection: The Isaiah apocalypse begins with the earth emptied, and every distinction of rank cancelled by the same judgment: 'as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master… as with the creditor, so with the debtor.' The earth 'polluted under its inhabitants, because they have… broken the everlasting covenant' — C01's moral order reaching the ground itself. Every source of mirth ceases, which is C18's lesson written across a whole world.

entries.pericope: He will wipe away tears from off all faces
entries.connection: 'You have been a stronghold to the poor, a stronghold to the needy in his distress.' Then the feast on the mountain 'for all peoples… He will destroy… the veil that is spread over all nations. He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces.' C27's widest circle, C19's final healing, and C16's poor at its foundation. Revelation 21:4 takes its words from here. The oracle against Moab that closes the chapter (25:10-12) is part of the pericope's argument and not what it anchors.

entries.pericope: You will keep whoever's mind is steadfast in perfect peace… Come, my people, enter into your rooms, and shut your doors
entries.connection: 'You will keep whoever's mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you' — C22's quiet soul in its most quoted form. 'With my soul have I desired you in the night' is C09's longing. And at the end, an instruction that Matthew 6:6 echoes: 'Come, my people, enter into your rooms, and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourself for a little moment.' The confession in the middle is unusually honest: 'We have been with child. We have been in pain. We gave birth, it seems, only to wind.'

entries.pericope: A pleasant vineyard! I, Yahweh, am its keeper… Let him make peace with me
entries.connection: The second song of the vineyard answers the first (5:1-7). Now the keeper says, 'I will water it every moment. Lest anyone damage it, I will keep it night and day. Wrath is not in me.' And to any who oppose it: 'let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me. Let him make peace with me.' 'Israel will blossom and bud. They will fill the surface of the world with fruit.' C11's vine tended rather than abandoned, and C15's peace offered twice to an adversary.

entries.pericope: This is the resting place. Give rest to weary… yet they would not hear
entries.connection: Priests and prophets 'reel with strong drink… They err in vision. They stumble in judgment.' They mock the prophet as if he were teaching infants — 'precept on precept… line on line, here a little, there a little' — the phrase is their parody, and the index does not build a doctrine of gradual teaching on it. What they refused is named plainly: 'This is the resting place. Give rest to weary… yet they would not hear.' C22's rest offered and declined, and C21's account of a judgment clouded at its source.

entries.pericope: I will make justice the measuring line, and righteousness the plumb line
entries.connection: The rulers have made 'a covenant with death… we have made lies our refuge.' Against it God lays a foundation: 'a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily' — the verse 1 Peter 2:6 applies to Christ. And the tools of the builder are moral: 'I will make justice the measuring line, and righteousness the plumb line.' C15's claim that peace is built, not found, with the builder's own instruments; and C08's exposure of a refuge built on lies.

entries.pericope: Does he who plows to sow plow continually?
entries.connection: A parable from the farm. The ploughman does not plough forever; he levels the ground and plants each seed in its place. Dill is beaten with a stick and cumin with a rod, not crushed under a cart wheel; 'bread flour must be ground; so he will not always be threshing it.' 'His God instructs him in right judgment.' Each crop handled according to its nature, each stage in its season — C25's growth that has its own times and cannot be forced, and C02's wisdom as a practical skill. The parable's point is that God's dealings are measured the same way.

entries.pericope: This people draws near with their mouth… but they have removed their heart far from me
entries.connection: 'This people draws near with their mouth and with their lips to honor me, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught.' Jesus quotes it in Matthew 15 against those who keep the tradition and break the command. C04's inconsistency between outward and inward, and C07's blindness — vision become 'like the words of a book that is sealed.' 'Who sees us? Who knows us?'

entries.pericope: The humble also will increase their joy in Yahweh… those who grumble will receive instruction
entries.connection: The reversal promised: the deaf hear, the blind see out of darkness, 'the humble also will increase their joy in Yahweh, and the poor among men will rejoice,' and those who set snares for the innocent in the gate are cut off. Even the complainers are included — 'those who err in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will receive instruction.' C19's healing and C16's poor.

entries.pericope: You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence. You refused
entries.connection: A people who 'tell the seers, Don't see! and to the prophets, Don't prophesy to us right things. Tell us pleasant things' — C08's false prophet, demanded by his audience. And the offer they refused, one of the great sentences of the prophets: 'You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence. You refused, but you said, No, for we will flee on horses.' C22's quiet soul offered as strategy, and declined for cavalry.

entries.pericope: Yahweh will wait, that he may be gracious to you… This is the way. Walk in it
entries.connection: 'Therefore Yahweh will wait, that he may be gracious to you.' Patience on God's side, and then guidance given in the middle of hardship: 'Though the Lord may give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your teachers won't be hidden anymore… your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, This is the way. Walk in it.' C19's waiting grace, and C08's true voice heard at the fork in the road. The day when 'Yahweh binds up the fracture of his people' ends the passage.

entries.pericope: A man shall be as a hiding place from the wind… as the shade of a large rock in a weary land
entries.connection: A king who reigns in righteousness, and a description of what a just person is to others: 'a hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the storm, as streams of water in a dry place, as the shade of a large rock in a weary land.' Against him, the fool who works 'to make empty the soul of the hungry,' and the scoundrel who destroys the humble 'even when the needy speaks right.' 'But the noble devises noble things.' C16's authority as shelter.

entries.pericope: The work of righteousness will be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever
entries.connection: The complacent — 'you women who are at ease… you careless daughters' — are warned of a failed harvest, and then the turn: 'until the Spirit is poured on us from on high.' Then justice in the wilderness, and the sentence that makes peace a consequence: 'The work of righteousness will be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.' C15's peace as something produced by right conduct, and C22's quiet as its fruit.

entries.pericope: Who among us can live with the devouring fire? He who walks righteously, and speaks blamelessly
entries.connection: 'Who among us can live with the devouring fire?' The answer is the same as Psalm 15's, and covers the Moral Audit's ground: one who 'walks righteously, and speaks blamelessly; who despises the gain of oppressions, who… refus[es] to take a bribe, who stops his ears from hearing of blood, and shuts his eyes from looking at evil.' Speech, money, and the guarded senses. C04's audit, and C07's eyes shut against what clouds them. Medium for PR01, as a list for self-examination rather than a command to perform it.

entries.pericope: Strengthen the weak hands… Tell those who have a fearful heart, Be strong. Don't be afraid
entries.connection: The desert blossoms, the blind see, the lame leap, and in the middle of the vision a command to the reader: 'Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Tell those who have a fearful heart, Be strong. Don't be afraid.' Verbal Almsgiving is seeking out the discouraged and giving them a good word, treated as real charity; this is the command to do it, quoted in Hebrews 12:12. Medium, because the verse is addressed to everyone, while the practice stresses the alms of those who have only words to give. The road through the restored wilderness is called 'The Holy Way… for those who walk in the Way' — the name the Didache and C01 give to the whole road.

entries.pericope: Hezekiah… went up to Yahweh's house, and spread it before Yahweh
entries.connection: The Assyrian envoy taunts the city in its own language from below the wall; the king's officers 'remained silent, and said nothing in reply, for the king's commandment was, Don't answer him.' Hezekiah tears his clothes, and when the threatening letter comes, he takes it into the temple 'and spread it before Yahweh' and prays. The threat carried into the place of prayer and laid open there is C09's; the refusal to answer the taunting is C22's quiet under provocation. Absorbing the Blow shares the silence but adds the inward pity for the angry one, which is not here, so PR18 is not tagged.

entries.pericope: I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears… you have cast all my sins behind your back
entries.connection: Told he will die, Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, prays, and weeps bitterly. 'I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears.' The psalm he writes afterward is a lament remembered from the far side: 'In the middle of my life I go into the gates of Sheol… I moaned like a dove. My eyes weaken looking upward. Lord, I am oppressed. Be my security.' And its resolution: 'you have in love for my soul delivered it from the pit… for you have cast all my sins behind your back.' Sacred Lament, and C28's numbered days — fifteen years added, each one known to be a gift.

entries.pericope: There is nothing among my treasures that I have not shown them… there will be peace and truth in my days
entries.connection: Flattered by envoys from Babylon, Hezekiah shows them everything — 'the silver, and the gold, the spices… all the house of his armor… There was nothing in his house… that Hezekiah didn't show them.' The reach for an admiring audience, which is what the Hidden Life is practised against (medium, as with Babel and Shebna). And when told that all of it will be carried off and his own descendants made eunuchs in Babylon, his answer is relief: 'there will be peace and truth in my days.' C18's attachment to treasure, and C14's household failed at the point where it reaches beyond one's own lifetime.

entries.pericope: Comfort, comfort my people… He will feed his flock like a shepherd
entries.connection: The Book of Comfort opens on its own title: 'Comfort, comfort my people… Speak comfortably to Jerusalem… her iniquity is pardoned.' The voice in the wilderness, the road made level, and the contrast 1 Peter 1:24 quotes: 'The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever' — C18's transience set against what remains. And the image of God that C19 opens with: 'He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.'

entries.pericope: His understanding is unsearchable… those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength
entries.connection: 'Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand?… Who has directed the Spirit of Yahweh, or has taught him as his counselor?' The nations a drop in a bucket, the inhabitants of the earth like grasshoppers, the stars called each by name. Then the complaint answered — 'Why do you say, Jacob… My way is hidden from Yahweh?' — with the Discipline of Unknowing's ground: 'His understanding is unsearchable.' What follows is strength for the long road, C25's: 'those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength… They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint' — the last and least dramatic of the three, and the one that lasts.

entries.pericope: Don't you be afraid, for I am with you… The poor and needy seek water, and there is none
entries.connection: 'Don't you be afraid, for I am with you. Don't be dismayed, for I am your God… I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.' Addressed to 'you worm Jacob,' the small and despised. And then the needy specifically: 'The poor and needy seek water, and there is none. Their tongue fails for thirst. I, Yahweh, will answer them.' C19's presence in fear, and C16's poor as the first to be answered.

entries.pericope: He won't break a bruised reed. He won't quench a dimly burning wick
entries.connection: The first Servant Song. The servant brings justice to the nations without noise — 'He will not shout, nor raise his voice, nor cause it to be heard in the street' — which is C23's hidden manner. And his strength is gentleness with what is almost finished: 'He won't break a bruised reed. He won't quench a dimly burning wick.' C27's mature mercy as the refusal to finish off the fragile. Matthew 12:18-21 applies it to Christ. 'To open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon.'

entries.pericope: You see many things, but don't observe. His ears are open, but he doesn't listen
entries.connection: 'Who is blind, but my servant?… You see many things, but don't observe. His ears are open, but he doesn't listen.' Sight and hearing intact and attention absent, which is C07's diagnosis. The judgment fell, and 'it burned him, but he didn't take it to heart' — the failure to trace a consequence back to its cause that C21 exists to correct.

entries.pericope: I have called you by your name. You are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you
entries.connection: 'Don't be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you… When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned.' Not exemption from the waters and the fire but company in them — C19's presence and C22's quieted fear. 'You have been precious and honored in my sight, and I have loved you.'

entries.pericope: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins
entries.connection: 'Don't remember the former things… Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs forth now. Don't you know it?' — C25's growth as something new springing up rather than the past repeated. Against the people's weariness and sins — 'you have burdened me with your sins. You have wearied me with your iniquities' — the line that defines the door of C19: 'I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.'

entries.pericope: Isn't there a lie in my right hand?
entries.connection: The satire of the idol-maker: he cuts a tree, burns half to bake his bread and warm himself — 'Aha! I am warm' — and carves the other half into a god and prays to it, 'Deliver me; for you are my god!' 'No one thinks, neither is there knowledge nor understanding to say, I have burned part of it in the fire… Shall I bow down to a tree trunk?' The question that would free him is never asked: 'A deceived heart has turned him aside; and he can't deliver his soul, nor say, Isn't there a lie in my right hand?' Interior Diagnosis is that question, and this is a portrait of its absence. C07's blindness self-inflicted, and C21's self-deception.

entries.pericope: I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, your transgressions… Return to me, for I have redeemed you
entries.connection: The order of the sentence matters: 'I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, your transgressions, and, as a cloud, your sins. Return to me, for I have redeemed you.' Redemption first, return second — not 'return so that I may redeem you.' C19's door, open before anyone walks through it. The heavens and the forests are told to sing about it.

entries.pericope: Most certainly you are a God who hides yourself… Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth
entries.connection: God names a foreign king his anointed — 'though you have not known me' — and asserts a sovereignty beyond human categories: 'I form the light, and create darkness. I make peace, and create calamity.' 'Woe to him who strives with his Maker — a clay pot among the clay pots of the earth!' And the confession of the nations: 'Most certainly you are a God who hides yourself.' The Discipline of Unknowing at its sharpest — God hidden even in self-revelation — and C24's ground. Then the widest invitation in the Old Testament, C27's: 'Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth… to me every knee shall bow' (the line Philippians 2:10 applies to Christ).

entries.pericope: Even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs will I carry you
entries.connection: The gods of Babylon are carried on the backs of animals, 'a burden to the weary,' and bow down with their idols into captivity. Israel's God reverses the direction: 'you that have been borne from your birth, that have been carried from the womb; and even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs will I carry you. I have made, and I will bear.' C18's idols as burdens one must carry, and C19's God who carries.

entries.pericope: You showed them no mercy; on the aged you have very heavily laid your yoke… I am, and there is none else besides me
entries.connection: Babylon is brought down to sit in the dust, and the charge is specific: 'you showed them no mercy; on the aged you have very heavily laid your yoke.' Its pride is quoted twice — 'I shall be a mistress forever… I am, and there is none else besides me' — and its cleverness named as the cause: 'your wisdom and your knowledge, it has perverted you.' C22's pride and C16's power without mercy.

entries.pericope: I have chosen you in the furnace of affliction… Oh that you had listened! Then your peace would have been like a river
entries.connection: A people who swear by God's name 'but not in truth, nor in righteousness,' told that their affliction was a furnace, not a rejection: 'Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of affliction' — C25's refining. And the longing of God for what obedience would have given: 'Oh that you had listened to my commandments! then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea.' C01's grain — the way things are made to go — stated as a lament. 'There is no peace, says Yahweh, for the wicked.'

entries.pericope: I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing… yet surely the justice due to me is with Yahweh
entries.connection: The second Servant Song: a servant 'hidden' in the shadow of God's hand, kept close 'in his quiver.' And his honest assessment of his own work: 'I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely the justice due to me is with Yahweh, and my reward with my God.' Faithfulness that sees no result and leaves the accounting to God is C23's hidden life. The answer enlarges the commission rather than explaining the failure: 'It is too light a thing… I will also give you for a light to the nations' — C27's circle.

entries.pericope: Can a woman forget her nursing child?… I have engraved you on the palms of my hands
entries.connection: 'But Zion said, Yahweh has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me.' The complaint is one sentence, and the answer is one of the tenderest in scripture: 'Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you! Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands.' Sacred Lament answered rather than rebuked. C19's God who remembers.

entries.pericope: That I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary… I gave my back to the strikers
entries.connection: The third Servant Song. 'The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary: he wakens morning by morning, he wakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.' Verbal Almsgiving in its most exact scriptural statement — a word given to the weary, and the listening that comes first, renewed every morning. Then the cost of the vocation, met without return: 'I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn't hide my face from shame and spitting.' Non-Retaliation, with its ground: 'the Lord Yahweh will help me… who is he who shall condemn me?' C03's hardest turn and C27's summit, in a single servant. 'He who walks in darkness, and has no light, let him trust in the name of Yahweh.'

entries.pericope: Who are you, that you are afraid of man who shall die?
entries.connection: 'Look to the rock you were cut from.' 'Don't fear the reproach of men, neither be dismayed at their insults' — C17's posture toward a hostile public. And the question that dissolves the fear: 'I, even I, am he who comforts you: who are you, that you are afraid of man who shall die, and of the son of man who shall be made as grass; and have forgotten Yahweh your Maker?' C22's quiet soul, grounded in an accurate sense of scale.

entries.pericope: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace
entries.connection: Jerusalem has drunk the cup of staggering, and 'there is none to guide her among all the sons whom she has brought forth; neither is there any who takes her by the hand.' God takes the cup out of her hand. 'You were sold for nothing; and you shall be redeemed without money.' And the messenger: 'How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace.' C19's redemption, and C15's peace announced.

entries.pericope: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn't open his mouth… and made intercession for the transgressors
entries.connection: The fourth Servant Song. 'He has no good looks or majesty… He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering' — C23's hiddenness taken to its limit. The observers misread the suffering exactly as Job's friends did: 'we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions… by his wounds we are healed' — C19's healing through another's wound. Under oppression he does not answer: 'as a lamb that is led to the slaughter… so he didn't open his mouth' — Non-Retaliation in silence. And at the end, the summit of Shedding Harshness: he 'bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.' The New Testament reads every line of it of Christ; the index anchors what the passage itself enacts.

entries.pericope: You shall forget the shame of your youth; and the reproach of your widowhood you shall remember no more
entries.connection: 'Sing, barren… Enlarge the place of your tent.' A wife cast off is called back: 'For a small moment have I forsaken you; but with great mercies will I gather you… For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed; but my loving kindness shall not depart from you.' And the restoration is complete, not probationary: 'you shall forget the shame of your youth; and the reproach of your widowhood you shall remember no more.' Merciful Reintegration is receiving back without lingering shame; this passage names the shame and promises it will not be remembered. God's practice, which the human practice imitates — medium for that reason, as at Psalm 103.

entries.pericope: Why do you spend money for that which is not bread?… For my thoughts are not your thoughts
entries.connection: 'Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat!' Grace offered free to the one who cannot pay — C19's. Then the question C18 asks of every life: 'Why do you spend money for that which is not bread? and your labor for that which doesn't satisfy?' The call to return — 'let the wicked forsake his way… and he will abundantly pardon' — is grounded in the distance between God and the one returning: 'For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways… as the heavens are higher than the earth.' The Discipline of Unknowing as the reason mercy can be larger than we expect. 'My word… shall not return to me void.'
